As of 255 AM EDT Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...An active weather pattern begins today and 
lasts through Saturday. The severe weather threat peaks today, 
with all modes of severe weather possible late this afternoon 
through this evening. The threat from periodic locally heavy 
rainfall begins this evening and continues into the upcoming 
weekend.

Latest analysis reveals the well-advertised cold front 
extending from the Eastern Great Lakes back into central IN/IL 
as of this writing. The front will reach the Mason-Dixon Line by
the early afternoon.

An upper-level low pivoting across SE Canada will amplify a 
broad trough over the Eastern CONUS. Multiple shortwaves 
tracking through the base of the trough from the Ohio Valley 
into the Mid-Atlantic tonight through Saturday will drive a 
strong cold front toward the region. Increasing clouds and some 
showers will be possible over far northern portions of our area 
from the Northern Neck to the Eastern Shore by late morning. How
far south these clouds can push will be a crucial piece 
regarding afternoon destabilization potential.

The severe weather threat will be fairly short-lived, but could
evolve rapidly late this afternoon and evening. A weak surface 
low is progged to develop along a lee trough just north of 
Richmond, tracking across the Northern Neck and MD Eastern 
Shore. Storms should initiate along the lee trough in the 
Piedmont before moving east into higher instability (MLCAPE 
15002000 J/kg east of I-95) and strong 3040 kt deep-layer 
shear. Initial discrete to semi-discrete cells will quickly 
consolidate into more of a QLCS/bowing line segment storm mode 
as outflow interacts with line-parallel flow focused along the 
boundary. This initial transition to a more linear mode poses 
the highest brief tornado threat, particularly from north of RIC
to Tappahannock and Salisbury, a narrow corridor where 
boundary-relative 01 km SRH is maximized. Thereafter, cold-pool
dominant processes will take over, with the main hazard 
transitioning to straight-line damaging winds and heavy rainfall
as forcing pushes the front east. It will be during this time 
frame that a transition to more protracted hydro concern begins.
In terms of severe weather outlook, the SPC has expanded their 
D1 Slight Risk to cover most of our area, with the exception of 
far SE VA and NE NC, which remains in a Marginal Risk area.

Regarding heavy rainfall potential, slow frontal progression 
increases confidence in several waves of heavy rain Thursday 
through Saturday. PWATs rebound to 2.0-2.3", supporting 
efficient rainfall rates along the stalled boundary. Broad 
forcing for ascent increases this afternoon and evening with the
initial shortwave, expanding thunderstorm coverage. While 
localized 3"/3hr HREF probabilities have pushed a bit farther 
north, away from the local area, there is nevertheless a very 
consistent QPF footprint from the past several runs of CAMS 
showing localized flash flooding potential along the coast of 
eastern VA and over the Eastern shore, coincident with 
convection and a developing theta-e ridge. Slow moving storms 
producing locally heavy rainfall will likely produce at least 
localized issues tonight into Friday morning, most likely in 
urban and poor-drainage areas. 

The front lingers over the region Friday before pushing 
offshore Saturday. Once again, the local area will be downstream
of the slow-moving trough axis on Friday, with at least a 
couple of rounds of convection persisting along coastal areas. 
CAMs have remained remarkably consistent with their heavy rain 
signal over the local area, with the greatest heavy rain threat 
shifting into the Carolinas, including south central/SE VA and 
NE NC locally, as the upper trough axis digs farther SE into the
mid-south by Friday evening, diving another front toward the 
local area. Meanwhile, the initial front will still be draped 
along the coast Saturday morning. The approaching front and the 
stalled front to the SE will each be the focus for additional 
rounds of scattered showers and storms inland, and numerous to 
widespread convection along the coast through Sat evening. 

WPC Excessive Rainfall Outlooks continue to outlook the entire 
area today, with a Marginal risk along and west of I-95 and into
NC, with a Slight Risk over the VA coast and Eastern Shore. A 
Slight Risk is in place for much of the area tomorrow, with the 
exception of a Marginal Risk far NW counties. And a Marginal 
Risk is in place for most of the area east of I-95 on Saturday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Mainly dry with seasonable temperatures Sunday
through Tuesday.

Model ensembles remain in good agreement that the main upper trough
axis shifts offshore by Sunday, driving the cold front south and
east of the region. In its wake, surface high pressure builds over
the Mid-Atlantic, introducing a drier air mass and seasonable
temperatures through early next week.
